families.topic: DAT indications, urgent treatment, dosage, intravenous administration, hypersensitivity and antimicrobial therapy
evidence_points: Diphtheria antitoxin is used to treat suspected or confirmed clinically appropriate toxigenic diphtheria.
Early treatment is important because benefit decreases as illness duration increases.
Classic respiratory diphtheria may require antitoxin before laboratory confirmation.
DAT is not used as prophylaxis for contacts.
Contact management instead uses vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis under national guidance.
Dosage depends on disease site, severity and duration rather than patient age alone.
Intravenous administration is preferred, especially for severe disease.
Because DAT is equine-derived, administration requires assessment and monitoring for hypersensitivity.
Appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be started alongside antitoxin treatment.
Antitoxin decisions require clinical presentation, toxigenic risk, illness duration and infectious-disease specialist input.

families.source: UKHSA general immunoglobulin product and administration guidance
families.topic: immunoglobulin product sourcing, storage, routes, administration and disease-specific limitations
families.page_title: General product information and how to administer immunoglobulin (issued August 2020)
evidence_points: UKHSA-issued immunoglobulin products are prepared from pooled non-UK donor plasma.
Donor and manufacturing controls are used to reduce recognised blood-borne infection risks.
Normal and disease-specific immunoglobulin products have different indications.
Some products are centrally held and issued through the Rabies and Immunoglobulin Service.
Administration route and dose depend on the disease-specific guidance and available product.
Large intramuscular volumes may need to be divided between injection sites.
Vaccine and immunoglobulin can require separate anatomical sites when co-administered.
Product licensing and the recommended public-health use may not always be identical.
Immunoglobulin gives short-term passive protection and does not replace vaccination when vaccination is indicated.
Safe use requires the exact product, concentration, route, timing, contraindications and disease-specific assessment.

families.source: UKHSA patient information on disease prevention using immunoglobulin
families.topic: purpose, timing, effectiveness, administration and limits of immunoglobulin prophylaxis
families.page_title: Information for patients on the prevention of diseases using immunoglobulin
evidence_points: Immunoglobulin is a medicinal product made from human plasma and contains antibodies.
It can be used after exposure when immediate short-term protection is needed.
Normal immunoglobulin contains a mixture of antibodies.
Disease-specific immunoglobulin contains higher levels of antibody to a particular infection.
Immunoglobulin works quickly but protection generally lasts for only a limited period.
Vaccines take longer to act but can provide longer-term immune memory.
Some exposed people require both vaccine and immunoglobulin.
Timing after exposure affects whether immunoglobulin can provide benefit.
Administration route and side-effect advice depend on the specific product.
Immunoglobulin is not automatically indicated after every exposure and requires a disease-specific assessment.

families.topic: mpox contact classification, risk assessment, follow-up, isolation and public-health advice
evidence_points: The guidance supports risk assessment and follow-up of contacts of confirmed mpox cases.
Contacts are categorised according to the nature and intensity of exposure.
Contact classification determines the public-health and isolation advice offered.
Direct skin or mucosal contact with lesions or contaminated material can be relevant.
Household, sexual, healthcare and other close-contact settings require different contextual assessment.
Follow-up advice includes monitoring for compatible symptoms during the relevant period.
Selected contacts may be considered for post-exposure vaccination.
Personal protective equipment can modify healthcare exposure risk.
Being in the same setting as a case does not automatically make a person a high-risk contact.
Classification requires confirmed-case timing, contact type, duration, barriers, contamination and individual vulnerability.

families.source: UKHSA guidance on when to suspect a case of mpox
families.topic: mpox clinical assessment, epidemiological criteria, testing, reporting, IPC and self-isolation
families.page_title: Mpox: guidance on when to suspect a case of mpox
evidence_points: The guidance describes clinical and epidemiological criteria that should prompt consideration of mpox.
Mpox can be caused by clade I or clade II MPXV.
Clinical assessment should consider rash or lesions alongside systemic and site-specific symptoms.
Travel, sexual contact, household contact and other epidemiological links can inform suspicion.
Clinicians should test for MPXV through an appropriate diagnostic pathway.
Alternative diagnoses should also be investigated when clinically appropriate.
Admitted patients require infection prevention and control measures.
People not requiring admission may need advice to self-isolate and reduce transmission.
Since 2025 neither clade I nor clade II mpox is managed as an HCID solely on clade classification.
A compatible rash alone does not confirm mpox; diagnosis requires appropriate testing and clinical assessment.
